anchor.quote: Use conjunctions to connect words, phrases and clauses.

not_rules.note: An instruction-shaped introduction to the function of conjunctions. It does not identify when a conjunction is required; treating every connection without one as a violation would invent a broader restriction.

anchor.quote: Coordinating conjunctions join things of equal importance

not_rules.note: Describes the grammatical function of coordinating conjunctions rather than stating a separate textual requirement.

anchor.quote: Coordinating conjunctions can also join clauses that could stand alone as sentences.

covers.quote: Some conjunctions come in pairs, such as ‘whether/or’, 'both/and', ‘either/or’ and ‘neither/nor’.

parts.quote: Whether wet or dry, the weather won't stop us going ahead with the team-building exercise.
My manager and I discussed both my performance review and my career prospects.
Either we complete the report today, or we work on it tomorrow.

rules.quote: Each conjunction in the pair should appear before the same type of word, phrase or clause.
rules.violation_condition: The members of a paired conjunction introduce different grammatical types, such as a noun phrase after one member and a clause after the other.
when: Applies to paired conjunctions, including whether/or, both/and, either/or and neither/nor.
rules.why: G-2: the different conjunction pairs are cases of one grammatical-parallelism check.

covers.quote: Conjunctive adverbs are often not needed.

parts.quote: The deadline was still weeks away; however, it was going to be tough to meet.
The deadline was still weeks away. It was going to be tough to meet.

rules.quote: They add nuance to writing, but use them sparingly.
rules.specification: The instruction concerns conjunctive adverbs. The manual supplies no frequency threshold for ‘sparingly’, so a checker needs an agreed interpretation of excessive use. An individual conjunctive adverb is not automatically a violation.
rules.violation_condition: A passage contains excessive conjunctive adverbs, particularly where they can be omitted without making the meaning unclear.
when: Conjunctive adverbs can add nuance; their presence alone does not establish excessive use.
rules.why: G-4: retain one sparing-use instruction; E-1: both versions in the example are compliant, not a correct/incorrect contrast.

parts.quote: The lake has had several blue-green algae outbreaks this year. It has been closed to swimming at least once a year since 2002.
The lake has had several blue-green algae outbreaks this year, with the lake closed to swimming at least once a year since 2002.

rules.quote: Don’t use ‘with’ to add a clause at the beginning or end of a sentence.
rules.violation_condition: ‘With’ introduces an added clause at the beginning or end of a sentence as though it were a conjunction.
when: Applies to clause-adding uses of ‘with’ at the beginning or end of a sentence, not ordinary prepositional uses.
rules.why: G-4: the body supplies the actionable restriction behind the descriptive heading; rewording and splitting are remedies, not separate checks.
